<reason>Side B (PRO) won a well-matched debate. B's opening option-value framing was coherent despite clipping, and its first rebuttal did the most damage of the round: the arithmetic showing fusion's few billions are a rounding error against energy-sector spending gutted CON's load-bearing opportunity-cost argument, while the "grid lock-in runs through 2070" and "prototype in the 2030s rests on research today" responses blunted A's timing attack. B handled both pressure questions directly with A1/A2 labels, offering a stagnation-based failure condition and accepting today's spending as a cap, which defused A's "option with no expiry" pressure. A performed well — the fission-in-fifteen-years audit comparison, the "faith, not finance" line, and the talent/political-capital reply to budget coexistence were genuinely sharp — but A's response to the scale rebuttal rested on assertions about scarce engineers and political capital that B plausibly contested, and A's own concession of "modest plasma science" narrowed the gap between the sides without a clear criterion for where the line sits. B's closing "what standard are we applying" frame plus "the decades pass either way" crystallized the clash more decisively than A's recap-flavored closing. Both sides were disciplined on evidence with no fake sourcing; the clipped opening is a minor execution cost for B.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>Side B's Rebuttal 1 arithmetic move — fusion's few billion dollars cannot be what is starving wind, solar, and grid buildout when global energy investment exceeds two trillion and the real bottlenecks are permitting and transmission — attacked the foundation of CON's case, and B sustained that damage control through the "budgets coexist" answer in Rebuttal 2 and the "aesthetic impatience is a feeling, not a policy" crystallization.</best_rebuttal>
